extracted.intended_audience: employers, industry stakeholders, OSHA rule commenters, and workplace safety/compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted requirements and analytic methods from OSHA's NPRM describing employer obligations and the agency's cost-estimation approach when the high-heat trigger is met or exceeded (rest breaks, observation, hazard alerts, warning signs, and related cost methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest Breaks at the High Heat Trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: All affected establishments would need to provide affected employees with rest breaks when the high heat trigger is met or exceeded. These rest breaks are different from those at the initial heat trigger in that they are scheduled, reoccurring at least every two hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees would still be allowed if-needed rest breaks as outlined under the initial heat trigger requirements, although OSHA estimates those if-needed rest breaks would be shorter when the high heat trigger is met or exceeded because affected employees would also receive scheduled rest breaks. OSHA estimates total high heat trigger rest break costs by estimating the number of hours by work shift type (daytime, evening, and overnight) in a given State that meets or exceeds the high heat trigger and normalizing these estimates to 8-hour work shift equivalents; these 8-hour work shift equivalents are then multiplied by the number of affected employees and the unit costs for both indoor and outdoor work conditions. See section VIII.C.IV.E.I. and appendix A for additional detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest Breaks at the Initial Heat Trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement category present in the analysis (tables) for providing rest breaks when the initial heat trigger is met (indoor and outdoor), with associated estimated costs by industry and region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA provides detailed tables of annualized one-time, annual, and total annualized costs for rest breaks at the initial heat trigger (separately for indoor and outdoor work) by industry category and region, discounted and undiscounted. Costs are calculated using work-shift equivalents and unit costs (see cost calculation method rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation for Signs and Symptoms at the High Heat Trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: When the high heat trigger is met or exceeded, designated person(s) must observe workers for signs and symptoms of heat-related illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA calculates total costs for observing signs and symptoms by multiplying the unit costs for both the designated person and at-risk worker by the number of affected employees and the number of 8-hour work shift equivalents. The method to calculate the number of work-shift equivalents is the same approach used in the calculation of total costs for rest breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard Alert (Notifying Employees of High Heat Conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must notify employees of high heat conditions (hazard alert) when the high heat trigger is met or exceeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA calculates total costs for notifying employees of high heat conditions using 8-hour work shift equivalents; those equivalents are multiplied by the number of affected establishments and the corresponding unit cost for a designated person to perform this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning Signs for Excessively High Heat Areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of warning signs for areas with excessively high heat is required, but OSHA assumed applicability only to industries with radiant heat sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To calculate total costs, OSHA multiplies the number of affected establishments with radiant heat sources by the unit cost for a warning sign and multiplies the number of affected establishments by the unit cost for a designated person to place that warning sign. This requirement is limited in the analysis to industries assumed to have radiant heat sources (per OSHA, 2024c and section VIII.C.IV.E.IV.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Communication—Supervisor
rubrics_metrics.description: A requirement category captured as 'Effective Communication—Supervisor' with associated estimated costs (tables) for communicating heat-related requirements/alerts to supervisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA provides tables of costs (annualized one-time, annual, total annualized) by industry and region for this communication requirement. The document presents totals for 'Effective Communication—Supervisor' (annualized and annual costs) though detailed procedural text for the communication method may be located elsewhere in the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Communication—Employee
rubrics_metrics.description: A requirement category captured as 'Effective Communication—Employee' with associated estimated costs (tables) for communicating heat-related requirements/alerts to employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA provides tables of costs (annualized one-time, annual, total annualized) by industry and region for this communication requirement. The document presents totals for 'Effective Communication—Employee' (annualized and annual costs) though detailed procedural text for the communication method may be located elsewhere in the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Calculation Method—Use of 8-Hour Work Shift Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's economic analysis normalizes estimated exposure hours to 8-hour work shift equivalents and uses those equivalents to scale unit costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, OSHA estimates the number of hours by work shift type (daytime, evening, overnight) meeting/exceeding the trigger, normalizes to 8-hour equivalents, and then multiplies those equivalents by the number of affected employees and the unit costs for each requirement (e.g., rest breaks, observation). For some requirements (eg., hazard alerts), OSHA multiplies 8-hour work shift equivalents by number of affected establishments and the unit cost for a designated person. This normalization method is used consistently across rest breaks, observation, and hazard alert cost calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic Assumption—Partial Offset from Reduced Pacing (Productivity Gains)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA assumes that a reduction in time spent on pacing (i.e., an increase in worker efficiency) will partially offset added costs of rest breaks when the high heat trigger is met or exceeded for affected workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA applies this partial-offset assumption differently by baseline non-compliance groups: for Group 1 (currently noncompliant with if-needed rest breaks and scheduled rest breaks), increase in efficiency partially offsets if-needed and scheduled rest break costs; for Group 2 (noncompliant with only scheduled rest breaks), increase in efficiency partially offsets scheduled rest break costs. Combining this offset with industry/state-level employee counts, baseline non-compliance rates, and state-level exposure, OSHA estimates that approximately 71.72 percent of the total cost of compliance with rest breaks when the high heat trigger is met or exceeded could be offset (approx. $9.92 billion out of $13.83 billion). This is an explicit modelling/assumption used in the cost totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data Limitation and Geographic Applicability Note (Alaska example)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA notes data limitations that affect applicability of the high heat trigger requirements and cost estimates in some locations (example: Alaska).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's best available evidence showed no days exceeding the high heat trigger in Alaska, and therefore the agency estimated most industries in Alaska will not have costs of compliance for requirements at or above the high heat trigger. OSHA acknowledges this may understate effects in establishments where employees are exposed to process heat, identified no data to adjust for that, and explicitly 'welcomes comment on the issue.' This functions as an acknowledgement of uncertainty/limitation in the analysis and an explicit invitation for public comment.
